translation_loss.what_was_lost: The translation shifts the grammatical structure of L3-L4. The Hindi 'mujhe jo paana chahta hai / vo dhoondhe mujhe' uses a relative-correlative structure ('jo... vo...') with a subjunctive/imperative nuance ('let them search for me' or 'should search for me'), which is flattened into a simple future declarative 'Those who seek me / Will find me' in English. Additionally, 'paana' (to obtain/reach/find) is translated as 'seek', collapsing the distinction between seeking and actually obtaining.

The grammatical gender of the speaker is explicitly marked as masculine in Hindi by the verb form 'khada hoon' (standing) in L1. The English translation 'I stand' is gender-neutral, losing this specific gender marker.

metaphor_spans.tenor: The speaker's state of absolute spiritual freedom, simplicity, and vital existence detached from material wealth.
metaphor_spans.vehicle: The vast sky and a single heartbeat as one's sole possessions.

translation_loss.what_was_lost: The relative pronoun 'jo' in L11 refers back to 'meri dhadkan' (my heartbeat) or 'ek aasman' (a sky), which are grammatically feminine and masculine respectively. The English translation uses 'it' in 'it is everywhere', which resolves the poetic ambiguity of whether the heartbeat, the sky, or the speaker's state is what is 'everywhere' into a single neutral pronoun.

original_poem:
पहाड़ पर मैं खड़ा हूँ
हवा के साथ, बादलों के बीच
मुझे जो पाना चाहता है
वो ढूँढे मुझे

धरती के रहस्य
जो भी शुद्ध मन से खोजे
वो मुझ तक पहुँचता है
हमेशा

मेरे पास कुछ नहीं है
बस एक आसमान है, मेरी धड़कन है
जो दुनिया से दूर है
और फिर भी हर कहीं है।
translated_poem:
On the Mountain, I Stand

I stand on the mountain,
With the wind, among the clouds,
Those who seek me
Will find me.

The secrets of the earth,
Whoever searches with a pure heart,
Will reach me
Always.

I have nothing,
Just a sky, my heartbeat,
Far from the world
And yet, it is everywhere.
